claim: Malaria resulted in 241 million cases of disease and over 600,000 deaths in 2020.
source: Malaria, caused by parasites of the genus Plasmodium, is a leading global driver of infection-related mortality, resulting in 241 million cases of disease and over 600,000 deaths in 2020 (World Malaria Report, 2021).
evidence: Cited from World Malaria Report, 2021

claim: Clinical immunity to malaria develops only after many years and repeated infections.
source: Clinical immunity to malaria (i.e. protection from symptoms) develops only after many years and repeated infections.
evidence: Referenced to multiple citations in the manuscript (Black et al., 2010; Schofield and Mueller, 2006; Ryg-Cornejo et al., 2016b)

claim: Children in endemic areas remain vulnerable to severe illness and death from malaria for several years.
source: Consequently, children in endemic areas remain vulnerable to severe illness and death for several years (Black et al., 2010; Schofield and Mueller, 2006; Ryg-Cornejo et al., 2016b)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Antibodies against P. falciparum in naturally exposed children are short-lived relative to antibodies against unrelated vaccine antigens.
source: For example, antibodies against P. falciparum in naturally exposed children are short-lived relative to antibodies against unrelated vaccine antigens (Portugal et al., 2013; Crompton et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Portugal et al., 2013 and Crompton et al., 2010

claim: P. falciparum infection has been linked to diminished T helper cell responses in children and adults.
source: and P. falciparum infection has been linked to diminished T helper cell responses in children and adults (Ho et al., 1986; Ho et al., 1988; Chizzolini et al., 1990; Rhee et al., 2001; Bejon et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Children with acute malaria exhibit impaired responses to a range of vaccinations.
source: children with acute malaria exhibit impaired responses to a range of vaccinations (Greenwood et al., 1972; Williamson and Greenwood, 1978)
evidence: Supported by citations to Greenwood et al., 1972 and Williamson and Greenwood, 1978

claim: Plasmodium infection causes declines in pre-existing, unrelated vaccine-induced antibodies and plasma cells in both mice and humans.
source: and Plasmodium infection causes declines in pre-existing, unrelated vaccine-induced antibodies and plasma cells in both mice and humans (Banga et al., 2015; Ng et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Banga et al., 2015 and Ng et al., 2014

claim: Some studies have found that P. falciparum-infected RBCs or parasite products can render human DCs refractory to activation and restrict priming of CD4+ T cells in vitro.
source: Some studies have found that P. falciparum-infected RBCs (iRBCs) or parasite products can render human DCs refractory to activation and restrict priming of CD4+ T cells in vitro (Urban et al., 1999; Pouniotis et al., 2004; Elliott et al., 2007; Yap et al., 2019; Millington et al., 2006; Pack et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to in vitro studies

claim: Humans with malaria have fewer and less activated circulating DCs than healthy controls.
source: and humans with malaria have fewer and less activated circulating DCs than healthy controls (Pinzon-Charry et al., 2013; Woodberry et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pinzon-Charry et al., 2013 and Woodberry et al., 2012

claim: Additional in vitro studies have concluded that DCs do become activated and can prime T cells after exposure to iRBCs and parasite products.
source: However, these decreases in circulating DCs during infection could reflect recruitment to infected tissues, and additional in vitro studies have concluded that DCs do become activated and can prime T cells after exposure to iRBCs and parasite products (Coban et al., 2005; Griffith et al., 2009; Götz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coban et al., 2005; Griffith et al., 2009; Götz et al., 2017

claim: B cells, rather than DCs, are the dominant antigen-presenting cells that direct activation and polarization of the CD4+ T cell response in mice with malaria.
source: Using more selective genetic tools to ablate antigen presentation specifically in DCs or B cells, we recently demonstrated that B cells, rather than DCs, are the dominant antigen-presenting cells (APCs) that direct activation and polarization of the CD4+ T cell response in mice with malaria (Arroyo and Pepper, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' previous work (Arroyo and Pepper, 2020)

claim: DCs were required for activating CD4+ T cell responses to a soluble protein antigen, whereas CD4+ T cell responses to the same antigen delivered on a nanoparticle required presentation by B cells.
source: Hong et al. showed recently that whereas DCs were required for activating CD4+ T cell responses to a soluble protein antigen, CD4+ T cell responses to the same antigen delivered on a nanoparticle required presentation by B cells (Hong et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hong et al., 2018

claim: DCs are relatively poor phagocytes of iRBCs.
source: We found that DCs are relatively poor phagocytes of iRBCs, which may be one contributing factor in the dominance of B cells as APCs in this disease.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2

claim: DCs remained competent to activate CD4+ T cell responses to soluble antigens in hosts with malaria.
source: We also found that DCs remained competent to activate CD4+ T cell responses to soluble antigens in hosts with malaria, suggesting no global dysfunction occurs.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4

claim: CD4+ T cell polarization, germinal center formation, and antibody production were profoundly altered during Plasmodium infection.
source: However, CD4+ T cell polarization, germinal center formation, and antibody production were profoundly altered, a finding that has implications for vaccination schemes in malaria-endemic regions.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in Figures 4 and 5

claim: Mice infected with P. yoelii developed an antigen-specific CD4+ T cell response that was strongly polarized to a T follicular helper cell (Tfh) phenotype.
source: We recently demonstrated that mice infected with the rodent-adapted parasite P. yoelii developed an antigen-specific CD4+ T cell response that was strongly polarized to a T follicular helper cell (Tfh) phenotype, specialized for assisting B cells with affinity maturation within germinal centers.
evidence: Refers to authors' previous work (Arroyo and Pepper, 2020)

claim: Antigen-specific T cells in mice with malaria possessed diminished proliferative capacity and longevity compared to T helper cells specific for the same epitope delivered in the context of an LCMV infection.
source: In mice with malaria, these antigen-specific T cells possessed diminished proliferative capacity and longevity compared to T helper cells specific for the same epitope delivered in the context of an LCMV infection.
evidence: Refers to authors' previous work (Arroyo and Pepper, 2020)

claim: DCs made up only a small fraction of total RBC+ splenocytes.
source: We found that DCs made up only a small fraction of total RBC+ splenocytes; instead, RBCs were mostly distributed between RPMs and B cells (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D

claim: RBCs were mostly distributed between RPMs and B cells.
source: We found that DCs made up only a small fraction of total RBC+ splenocytes; instead, RBCs were mostly distributed between RPMs and B cells (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D

claim: DCs bound similar frequencies of nRBCs and iRBCs.
source: In our in vivo experiments, DCs bound similar frequencies of nRBCs and iRBCs (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: B cells bound significantly more iRBCs than nRBCs both in vivo and in vitro.
source: Interestingly, B cells bound significantly more iRBCs than nRBCs both in vivo and in vitro (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Preferential binding of iRBCs by B cells was independent of the B cell receptor (BCR).
source: This experiment revealed that preferential binding of iRBCs was independent of the BCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data using MD4 transgenic B cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: B cells may selectively interact with iRBCs through antigen-independent pathways such as complement receptors, Fc receptors, or scavenger receptors.
source: leading us to speculate that B cells may selectively interact with iRBCs through other, antigen-independent pathways such as complement receptors, Fc receptors, or scavenger receptors (Vijay et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculation based on experimental observation and cited literature

claim: DCs accounted for around 10% of PE+ events, despite comprising only 1–2% of splenocytes.
source: However, DCs accounted for around 10% of PE+ events, despite comprising only 1–2% of splenocytes.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: The iRBC+ population included very few DCs (1–3%, commensurate with their total splenic frequency), but many more RPMs (~20%) in addition to B cells.
source: In contrast, the iRBC+ population included very few DCs (1–3%, commensurate with their total splenic frequency), but many more RPMs (~20%) in addition to B cells (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: Approximately 5% of CD11chi MHCIIhi splenic DCs had taken up IV-injected PE, whereas the percentage of DCs labeling with iRBCs was virtually zero.
source: Whereas ~5% of CD11chi MHCIIhi splenic DCs had taken up IV-injected PE, the percentage of DCs labeling with iRBCs was virtually zero (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D

claim: DCs capture a greater fraction of the total cell-associated PE than the total cell-associated iRBC signal.
source: However, DCs capture a greater fraction of the total cell-associated PE than the total cell-associated iRBC signal, indicating a better ability to capture PE (Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The ratio of PE+ DCs to iRBC+ DCs within each mouse was significantly higher than the ratio of PE+ RPMs or B cells to iRBC+ RPMs or B cells, respectively.
source: Further, the ratio of PE+ DCs to iRBC+ DCs within each mouse was significantly higher than the ratio of PE+ RPMs or B cells to iRBC+ RPMs or B cells, respectively, indicating that DCs are biased toward taking up PE more so than iRBCs, relative to the other APC subsets examined (Figure 2E).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: DCs do not capture iRBCs as efficiently as soluble antigen in vivo.
source: Thus, DCs do not capture iRBCs as efficiently as soluble antigen in vivo.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data from Figure 2

claim: The majority of iRBCs associate with other APC subsets, including B cells.
source: Instead, the majority of iRBCs associate with other APC subsets, including B cells.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data from Figures 1 and 2

claim: DCs from infected mice do acquire Plasmodium antigens in vivo.
source: It is possible that even a small amount of antigen uptake and presentation is sufficient to permit activation of naïve T cells, and indeed it has been shown that DCs from infected mice do acquire Plasmodium antigens in vivo (Pouniotis et al., 2004; Sponaas et al., 2012; Sponaas et al., 2006; Voisine et al., 2010; Perry et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Poor acquisition of iRBC-borne antigen may be one factor underlying the lack of substantial contribution from DCs to the antigen-specific CD4+ T cell response in Plasmodium-infected mice.
source: However, in light of our previous study identifying B cells as the primary APCs in mice with malaria (Arroyo and Pepper, 2020), as well as data showing that B cells preferentially present nanoparticle-associated antigens to T cells (Hong et al., 2018), we suggest that poor acquisition of iRBC-borne antigen may be one factor underlying the lack of substantial contribution from DCs to the antigen-specific CD4+ T cell response in Plasmodium-infected mice.
evidence: Inference based on current experimental data and cited literature

claim: Parasitemia was still ascending at day 5 post-infection with P. chabaudi.
source: As expected, we found that parasitemia was still ascending (Figure 3A)
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Total DC numbers in the spleen were not significantly different from naïve mice at day 5 post-infection.
source: but total DC numbers in the spleen were not significantly different from naïve mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Significantly higher frequencies of PE+ DCs were observed in infected compared to uninfected mice 30 min after injection.
source: 30 min after injection, we observed significantly higher frequencies of PE+ DCs in infected compared to uninfected mice (Figure 3C), indicating that there is no defect in acquisition of soluble antigen by DCs during infection.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: There is no defect in acquisition of soluble antigen by DCs during infection.
source: 30 min after injection, we observed significantly higher frequencies of PE+ DCs in infected compared to uninfected mice (Figure 3C), indicating that there is no defect in acquisition of soluble antigen by DCs during infection.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: B cell uptake of PE was slightly increased in infected versus uninfected mice, but the difference was not statistically significant.
source: B cell uptake of PE was slightly increased in infected versus uninfected mice, but the difference was not statistically significant (Figure 3D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs) were rare in the spleens of uninfected mice.
source: moDCs were rare in the spleens of uninfected mice.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F

claim: In infected mice, moDCs comprised approximately 30% of all DCs, but made up approximately 80% of PE+ DCs.
source: In infected mice, they comprised ~30% of all DCs, but made up ~80% of PE+ DCs (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F

claim: moDCs disproportionately capture the majority of soluble antigen in infected mice, compared to CD64- conventional DCs (cDCs).
source: Thus, moDCs disproportionately capture the majority of soluble antigen in infected mice, compared to CD64- conventional DCs (cDCs).
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F

claim: moDCs expressed at least as much MHCII as cDCs.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of surface markers revealed that moDCs expressed at least as much MHCII as cDCs, and had significantly higher expression of the costimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86 compared to cDCs from either uninfected or infected mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: moDCs had significantly higher expression of the costimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86 compared to cDCs from either uninfected or infected mice.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of surface markers revealed that moDCs expressed at least as much MHCII as cDCs, and had significantly higher expression of the costimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86 compared to cDCs from either uninfected or infected mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: moDCs possess the basic requirements for efficient T cell priming.
source: These moDCs express robust levels of MHCII and costimulatory molecules, and therefore possess the basic requirements for efficient T cell priming.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 3G and established immunological knowledge

claim: DC uptake of soluble antigen remains intact after 5 days of P. chabaudi infection.
source: Altogether, our data demonstrate that DC uptake of soluble antigen remains intact after 5 days of P. chabaudi infection, but that the antigen-capturing subset shifts primarily from cDCs to moDCs.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: The antigen-capturing DC subset shifts primarily from cDCs to moDCs after 5 days of P. chabaudi infection.
source: Altogether, our data demonstrate that DC uptake of soluble antigen remains intact after 5 days of P. chabaudi infection, but that the antigen-capturing subset shifts primarily from cDCs to moDCs.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: GP66-specific T cells were rare in unimmunized mice but expanded dramatically following immunization in both uninfected and infected mice.
source: GP66-specific T cells were rare in unimmunized mice but expanded dramatically following immunization in both uninfected and infected mice.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: No T cell expansion was observed in infected mice that did not receive GP.
source: No T cell expansion was observed in infected mice that did not receive GP.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: The total number of GP66-specific CD4+ T cells was not significantly different between uninfected and infected mice following immunization of both.
source: The total number of GP66-specific CD4+ T cells was not significantly different between uninfected and infected mice following immunization of both, indicating that the ability of DCs to present soluble antigen and activate T cells was roughly intact in infected mice (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: The ability of DCs to present soluble antigen and activate T cells was roughly intact in infected mice.
source: The total number of GP66-specific CD4+ T cells was not significantly different between uninfected and infected mice following immunization of both, indicating that the ability of DCs to present soluble antigen and activate T cells was roughly intact in infected mice (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: Uninfected mice immunized with GP developed a distinct population of GC Tfh cells, as well as a sizeable subset of CXCR5+ PD-1lo Tfh cells.
source: As expected, uninfected mice immunized with GP developed a distinct population of GC Tfh cells, as well as a sizeable subset of CXCR5+ PD-1lo Tfh cells.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: The Tfh and GC Tfh populations were virtually absent among GP66-specific cells in infected mice following GP immunization.
source: Strikingly, however, the Tfh and GC Tfh populations were virtually absent among GP66-specific cells in infected mice following GP immunization (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: Abundant CXCR5+ T cells were observed in the bulk (non-tetramer-binding) T cell population in infected mice.
source: This was not due to a generalized loss of Tfh cells in infected mice, since abundant CXCR5+ T cells were observed in the bulk (non-tetramer-binding) T cell population (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The total number of GP66-specific CD4+ T cells was still not significantly different between mice that had concurrent P. chabaudi infection and those that did not at 3-5 weeks post-immunization.
source: At these late timepoints, the total number of GP66-specific CD4+ T cells was still not significantly different between mice that had concurrent P. chabaudi infection and those that did not, although there was a nonsignificant trend toward higher T cell numbers in infected mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: The percentage of GP66-specific T cells exhibiting a GC Tfh phenotype remained sharply decreased in infected mice at 3-5 weeks post-immunization.
source: The percentage of GP66-specific T cells exhibiting a GC Tfh phenotype remained sharply decreased in infected mice (Figure 4F)
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: The absolute number of GP66-specific GC Tfh cells was not significantly different between infected and uninfected mice at 3-5 weeks post-immunization.
source: but the absolute number of GP66-specific GC Tfh cells was not significantly different between the two experimental groups, perhaps because of the slightly higher numbers of total GP66-specific T cells in the infected mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4G

claim: An established P. chabaudi infection does not prevent expansion of T cells in response to a heterologous soluble antigen.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that an established P. chabaudi infection does not prevent expansion of T cells in response to a heterologous soluble antigen, but does temporarily disrupt the polarization of antigen-specific T cells into B cell-helping Tfh and GC Tfh cells.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: An established P. chabaudi infection temporarily disrupts the polarization of antigen-specific T cells into B cell-helping Tfh and GC Tfh cells.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that an established P. chabaudi infection does not prevent expansion of T cells in response to a heterologous soluble antigen, but does temporarily disrupt the polarization of antigen-specific T cells into B cell-helping Tfh and GC Tfh cells.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: DCs can orchestrate initial differentiation of CXCR5+ Tfh cells 2–4 days after immunization.
source: Previous work has shown that DCs can orchestrate initial differentiation of CXCR5+ Tfh cells 2–4 days after immunization, but that maintenance of the Tfh phenotype at day 8 requires both cognate and non-cognate interactions with B cells (Kerfoot et al., 2011; Pepper et al., 2011; von der Weid and Langhorne, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kerfoot et al., 2011; Pepper et al., 2011; von der Weid and Langhorne, 1993

claim: Maintenance of the Tfh phenotype at day 8 requires both cognate and non-cognate interactions with B cells.
source: Previous work has shown that DCs can orchestrate initial differentiation of CXCR5+ Tfh cells 2–4 days after immunization, but that maintenance of the Tfh phenotype at day 8 requires both cognate and non-cognate interactions with B cells (Kerfoot et al., 2011; Pepper et al., 2011; von der Weid and Langhorne, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kerfoot et al., 2011; Pepper et al., 2011; von der Weid and Langhorne, 1993

claim: Interactions between DCs and T cells were intact in infected mice, allowing for T cell expansion.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that interactions between DCs and T cells were intact in infected mice, allowing for T cell expansion, but that infection disrupted interactions between GP-specific T cells and B cells, preventing establishment of Tfh and GC Tfh populations.
evidence: Hypothesis based on experimental data and cited literature

claim: Infection disrupted interactions between GP-specific T cells and B cells, preventing establishment of Tfh and GC Tfh populations.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that interactions between DCs and T cells were intact in infected mice, allowing for T cell expansion, but that infection disrupted interactions between GP-specific T cells and B cells, preventing establishment of Tfh and GC Tfh populations.
evidence: Hypothesis based on experimental data

claim: iRBC-associated GP66 is primarily presented by B cells.
source: Since iRBC-associated GP66 is primarily presented by B cells (Arroyo and Pepper, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Arroyo and Pepper, 2020

claim: Expansion of GP66-specific CD4+ T cells was defective in day 5-infected mice treated with irradiated iRBCs containing GP66+ P. yoelii parasites.
source: This was indeed what we observed (Figure 4H).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4H

claim: CXCR5+ Tfh and GC Tfh subsets were significantly diminished in infected mice treated with irradiated iRBCs containing GP66+ P. yoelii parasites.
source: CXCR5+ Tfh and GC Tfh subsets were also significantly diminished in infected mice, consistent with the loss of cognate and non-cognate B-T interactions that normally induce Tfh polarization (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4I and J

claim: In an infected spleen, DCs remain competent for uptake and presentation of soluble antigens.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that in an infected spleen, DCs remain competent for uptake and presentation of soluble antigens, but that the signals required for T cell polarization into Tfh cells—including both cognate and non-cognate interactions with B cells—are disrupted.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data from Figures 3 and 4

claim: The signals required for T cell polarization into Tfh cells—including both cognate and non-cognate interactions with B cells—are disrupted in an infected spleen.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that in an infected spleen, DCs remain competent for uptake and presentation of soluble antigens, but that the signals required for T cell polarization into Tfh cells—including both cognate and non-cognate interactions with B cells—are disrupted.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data from Figures 3 and 4

claim: GP-specific B cells expanded robustly in number 8 days after GP immunization of uninfected mice.
source: These cells expanded robustly in number 8 days after GP immunization of uninfected mice, but not following GP immunization of mice infected for 5 days with P. chabaudi (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: GP-specific B cells did not expand following GP immunization of mice infected for 5 days with P. chabaudi.
source: These cells expanded robustly in number 8 days after GP immunization of uninfected mice, but not following GP immunization of mice infected for 5 days with P. chabaudi (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: The frequency of CD138+ GP-specific plasmablasts was modest 8 days post-immunization and was not different between infected and uninfected mice.
source: The frequency of CD138+ GP-specific plasmablasts was modest 8 days post-immunization and was not different between infected and uninfected mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: A sizeable population of GP-specific GC B cells appeared in uninfected, immunized mice, but was greatly decreased in infected mice following immunization.
source: In contrast, a sizeable population of GP-specific GC B cells (CD138- CD38- GL7+) appeared in uninfected, immunized mice, but was greatly decreased in infected mice following immunization (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Plasmodium-specific GC B cells are readily detected at 13 days after infection.
source: Previous work from our group found that Plasmodium-specific GC B cells are readily detected at this time (i.e. 13 days after infection) (Krishnamurty et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krishnamurty et al., 2016

claim: Tfh cells are required to sustain the repeated rounds of proliferation and selection that antigen-specific B cells undergo in GCs.
source: These data identify a functional consequence of the drastic decrease in GP66-specific GC Tfh cells in infected mice, as Tfh cells are required to sustain the repeated rounds of proliferation and selection that antigen-specific B cells undergo in GCs.
evidence: Based on established immunological knowledge

claim: GP-specific serum IgG antibody titers were much lower in infected compared to uninfected mice 7 days after immunization.
source: Consistent with the decreases in total and GC B cell numbers, GP-specific serum IgG antibody titers were much lower in infected compared to uninfected mice 7 days after immunization (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5E and F

claim: A slight but significant defect in serum IgG persisted 14 days after immunization.
source: A slight but significant defect in serum IgG persisted 14 days after immunization
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5F

claim: After 3 weeks, antibody titers in infected mice increased to the levels of those in uninfected mice.
source: however, after 3 weeks, titers in infected mice increased to the levels of those in uninfected mice, consistent with our observation that absolute numbers of GP66-specific GC Tfh cells have recovered in infected mice at this stage (Figure 4G).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 4G

claim: Established Plasmodium infection significantly decreases expansion of B cells, establishment of germinal centers, and production of antibodies specific for a heterologous protein antigen.
source: These data show that established Plasmodium infection significantly decreases expansion of B cells, establishment of germinal centers, and production of antibodies specific for a heterologous protein antigen.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: Differential uptake is likely not the only factor biasing antigen presentation toward B cells during Plasmodium infection.
source: However, differential uptake is likely not the only factor biasing antigen presentation toward B cells, since DCs do acquire sufficient antigen in infected mice to activate CD4+ T cells ex vivo (Pouniotis et al., 2004; Sponaas et al., 2012; Sponaas et al., 2006; Voisine et al., 2010; Perry et al., 2004).
evidence: Inference based on current data and cited literature

claim: Some parasite antigen may be acquired by DCs in soluble form after being shed from iRBCs.
source: We speculate that some of this antigen may be acquired by DCs in soluble form after being shed from iRBCs (Beeson et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculation based on cited literature

claim: The CD8- CD11b+ DC subset from infected mice largely overlaps with the CD11b+ CD64+ moDC population identified as the main DC subset capturing soluble antigen in infected mice.
source: The use of different markers to define DC subsets complicates direct comparisons between our findings and previous studies, but Sponaas et al. identified CD8- CD11b+ DCs from infected mice as the most robust activators of CD4+ T cells ex vivo Sponaas et al., 2006; we believe that at the timepoints examined, this subset largely overlaps with the CD11b+ CD64+ moDC population that we identified here as the main DC subset capturing soluble antigen in infected mice.
evidence: Inference based on comparison with cited literature and current data

claim: moDCs have been found fully capable of antigen presentation and T cell activation in other contexts.
source: In other contexts, moDCs have been found fully capable of antigen presentation and T cell activation (Plantinga et al., 2013; Gieseler et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Plantinga et al., 2013 and Gieseler et al., 1998

claim: The splenic architecture undergoes profound alteration in mice and humans with malaria, with dissolution of marginal zones and blurring of borders between the T cell zones and B cell follicles.
source: This is important because the splenic architecture undergoes profound alteration in mice and humans with malaria, with dissolution of marginal zones and blurring of borders between the T cell zones and B cell follicles; it has been suggested that these architectural disruptions contribute to the observed delay in establishment of germinal centers, and subsequent failure to make optimal antibody responses (Achtman et al., 2003; Stevenson and Kraal, 1989; Beattie et al., 2006; Urban et al., 2005; Cadman et al., 2008; Keitany et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Architectural disruptions in the spleen contribute to the observed delay in establishment of germinal centers, and subsequent failure to make optimal antibody responses during malaria.
source: This is important because the splenic architecture undergoes profound alteration in mice and humans with malaria, with dissolution of marginal zones and blurring of borders between the T cell zones and B cell follicles; it has been suggested that these architectural disruptions contribute to the observed delay in establishment of germinal centers, and subsequent failure to make optimal antibody responses (Achtman et al., 2003; Stevenson and Kraal, 1989; Beattie et al., 2006; Urban et al., 2005; Cadman et al., 2008; Keitany et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Tissue changes in the spleen have already begun to occur 5 days after infection and reach their peak during the window in which the GP-specific response is being initiated.
source: These tissue changes have already begun to occur 5 days after infection, when we immunized mice with GP, and reach their peak during the window in which the GP-specific response is being initiated (Achtman et al., 2003; Stevenson and Kraal, 1989; Cadman et al., 2008; Ryg-Cornejo et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Even within a dramatically altered tissue environment, DCs are able to interact with both antigen and CD4+ T cells in a way that permits robust expansion of the latter.
source: Our data suggest that even within this dramatically altered tissue environment, DCs are able to interact with both antigen and CD4+ T cells in a way that permits robust expansion of the latter, ruling out the existence of global DC dysfunction in the malaria-inflamed spleen.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data from Figures 3 and 4

claim: There is no global DC dysfunction in the malaria-inflamed spleen.
source: Our data suggest that even within this dramatically altered tissue environment, DCs are able to interact with both antigen and CD4+ T cells in a way that permits robust expansion of the latter, ruling out the existence of global DC dysfunction in the malaria-inflamed spleen.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data from Figures 3 and 4

claim: The loss of GP-specific Tfh and GC Tfh cells in Plasmodium-infected mice is due to disruption of both cognate and non-cognate interactions between GP-specific T cells and B cells.
source: We and others previously showed that ICOS-mediated interactions between B and T cells support maintenance of Tfh cells, while cognate B-T interactions are necessary for the GC Tfh subset (Pepper et al., 2011). In light of this, we infer that the loss of GP-specific Tfh and GC Tfh cells in Plasmodium-infected mice is due to disruption of both cognate and non-cognate interactions between GP-specific T cells and B cells.
evidence: Inference based on current data and cited literature

claim: Alteration of the splenic architecture may play an important role in the loss of Tfh cells, with the blurring of the T-B border potentially making it more difficult for activated T cells to locate B cells.
source: Here, alteration of the splenic architecture may play an important role, with the blurring of the T-B border potentially making it more difficult for activated T cells to locate B cells.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental observations and known splenic architecture changes

claim: The inflammatory milieu of the infected spleen may negatively impact Tfh development.
source: The inflammatory milieu of the infected spleen may also negatively impact Tfh development; we and others have found that blocking inflammatory cytokines enhances the differentiation of Tfh cells and GC B cells during infections with other strains of Plasmodium (Keitany et al., 2016; Ryg-Cornejo et al., 2016a).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to Keitany et al., 2016 and Ryg-Cornejo et al., 2016a

claim: Blocking inflammatory cytokines enhances the differentiation of Tfh cells and GC B cells during infections with other strains of Plasmodium.
source: we and others have found that blocking inflammatory cytokines enhances the differentiation of Tfh cells and GC B cells during infections with other strains of Plasmodium (Keitany et al., 2016; Ryg-Cornejo et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Keitany et al., 2016 and Ryg-Cornejo et al., 2016a

claim: The BCR-independent binding of iRBCs may dilute or misdirect the antigen-specific B cell response in hosts with malaria.
source: Finally, it is interesting to speculate whether the BCR-independent binding of iRBCs that we observed may dilute or misdirect the antigen-specific B cell response in hosts with malaria.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental observations

claim: Plasmodium infection is known to induce polyclonal, nonspecific B cell activation as well as activation of B cells autoreactive for RBC antigens.
source: Indeed, Plasmodium infection is known to induce polyclonal, nonspecific B cell activation as well as activation of B cells autoreactive for RBC antigens (Rivera-Correa et al., 2020; Rivera-Correa et al., 2019; Fernandez-Arias et al., 2016; Sardinha et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Mice infected with LCMV simultaneous with or 4 days before heterologous immunization developed fewer immunogen-specific antibody-secreting cells and lower specific antibody titers.
source: Daugan et al. previously found that mice infected with LCMV simultaneous with or 4 days before heterologous immunization developed fewer immunogen-specific antibody-secreting cells and lower specific antibody titers, suggesting that other pathogens can induce similar immune dysfunction (Daugan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Daugan et al., 2016

claim: Mice infected with vesicular stomatitis virus had intact responses to heterologous immunization.
source: However, the same study found intact responses to heterologous immunization in mice infected with vesicular stomatitis virus, indicating that not all infections disrupt heterologous immunity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Daugan et al., 2016

claim: Mice infected with Plasmodium two days after heterologous immunization exhibited defective antibody responses to the heterologous antigen.
source: A separate study found that mice infected with Plasmodium two days after heterologous immunization exhibited defective antibody responses to the heterologous antigen, but immunized mice infected with LCMV or Listeria monocytogenes did not (Banga et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Banga et al., 2015

claim: Immunized mice infected with LCMV or Listeria monocytogenes did not exhibit defective antibody responses to the heterologous antigen.
source: A separate study found that mice infected with Plasmodium two days after heterologous immunization exhibited defective antibody responses to the heterologous antigen, but immunized mice infected with LCMV or Listeria monocytogenes did not (Banga et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Banga et al., 2015

claim: Multiple pathogenic infections can interfere with the robust development of heterologous responses.
source: Nevertheless, we favor the hypothesis that multiple pathogenic infections can interfere with the robust development of heterologous responses.
evidence: Hypothesis based on synthesis of cited literature

claim: The precise mechanisms of disruption of heterologous responses differ in different infections, but likely involve host-derived cytokines and chemokines.
source: The precise mechanisms of disruption appear to differ in different infections, but likely involve host-derived cytokines and chemokines, with type 1 interferons, lymphotoxin, and interferon gamma being implicated in studies using LCMV, Toxoplasma gondii, and Plasmodium respectively (Keitany et al., 2016; Daugan et al., 2016; Glatman Zaretsky et al., 2012).
evidence: Inference based on cited literature

claim: Type 1 interferons, lymphotoxin, and interferon gamma have been implicated in disruption of heterologous responses in studies using LCMV, Toxoplasma gondii, and Plasmodium respectively.
source: The precise mechanisms of disruption appear to differ in different infections, but likely involve host-derived cytokines and chemokines, with type 1 interferons, lymphotoxin, and interferon gamma being implicated in studies using LCMV, Toxoplasma gondii, and Plasmodium respectively (Keitany et al., 2016; Daugan et al., 2016; Glatman Zaretsky et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Keitany et al., 2016; Daugan et al., 2016; Glatman Zaretsky et al., 2012

claim: Defects in the humoral response correlate with elevated inflammation and disruption of the splenic architecture.
source: Typically in these studies, defects in the humoral response correlate with elevated inflammation and disruption of the splenic architecture; as inflammation resolves, the infection is cleared, and the tissue reorganizes, germinal centers and B cell responses also recover.
evidence: Generalization based on cited literature

claim: As inflammation resolves, the infection is cleared, and the tissue reorganizes, germinal centers and B cell responses also recover.
source: Typically in these studies, defects in the humoral response correlate with elevated inflammation and disruption of the splenic architecture; as inflammation resolves, the infection is cleared, and the tissue reorganizes, germinal centers and B cell responses also recover.
evidence: Generalization based on cited literature

claim: The majority of iRBCs associate with splenic B cells rather than with DCs.
source: By expanding previously established assays of iRBC uptake to include examination of B cells, we found that the majority of iRBCs associate with splenic B cells rather than with DCs, and that B cells preferentially bind iRBCs over nRBCs.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2

claim: B cells preferentially bind iRBCs over nRBCs.
source: By expanding previously established assays of iRBC uptake to include examination of B cells, we found that the majority of iRBCs associate with splenic B cells rather than with DCs, and that B cells preferentially bind iRBCs over nRBCs.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2

claim: B cells were the primary APCs that activated CD4+ T cell responses when antigen was delivered in nanoparticle form.
source: This finding is consistent with a previous study showing that B cells were the primary APCs that activated CD4+ T cell responses when antigen was delivered in nanoparticle form, whereas DCs were key for initiating responses to the same antigen in soluble form (Hong et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hong et al., 2018

claim: DCs were key for initiating responses to antigen in soluble form.
source: This finding is consistent with a previous study showing that B cells were the primary APCs that activated CD4+ T cell responses when antigen was delivered in nanoparticle form, whereas DCs were key for initiating responses to the same antigen in soluble form (Hong et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hong et al., 2018

claim: B cell uptake of nanoparticle-associated antigen was BCR-dependent and performed by antigen-specific B cells.
source: In that study, B cell uptake of nanoparticle-associated antigen was BCR-dependent and performed by antigen-specific B cells.
evidence: Refers to Hong et al., 2018

claim: B cells can preferentially bind iRBCs independent of the BCR.
source: Here, we found that B cells can preferentially bind iRBCs independent of the BCR, although this does not preclude additional BCR-dependent binding by B cells specific for parasite antigens, such as those we have characterized extensively in previous studies (Krishnamurty et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2019; Keitany et al., 2016; Thouvenel et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Selective but BCR-independent binding of iRBCs by B cells suggests the existence of antigen-nonspecific interactions between iRBCs and B cells that might explain the reported activation of nonspecific polyclonal or autoreactive B cells during malaria.
source: This selective but BCR-independent binding is intriguing; it suggests the existence of antigen-nonspecific interactions between iRBCs and B cells that might explain the reported activation of nonspecific polyclonal or autoreactive B cells during malaria.
evidence: Inference based on experimental observations

claim: Receptors expressed by B cells might bind opsonizing antibody, complement, exposed phosphatidylserines or parasite proteins on the iRBC surface.
source: The literature suggests a number of possible such interaction pathways: receptors expressed by B cells might bind opsonizing antibody, complement, exposed phosphatidylserines or parasite proteins on the iRBC surface (Vijay et al., 2021; Boyle et al., 2015; Donati et al., 2004).
evidence: Speculation based on cited literature

claim: iRBCs contain immunostimulatory ligands, such as parasite RNA and DNA, that could activate B cells through Toll-like receptor signaling.
source: Once taken up, iRBCs contain immunostimulatory ligands, such as parasite RNA and DNA, that could activate B cells through Toll-like receptor signaling, alone or in conjunction with signaling from any of the above pathways (Baccarella et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2010; Rivera-Correa et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculation based on cited literature

claim: The iRBCs used in this study were isolated from mice 6–7 days post-infection, a time when some anti-parasite antibody may be present on the iRBC surface.
source: The iRBCs used in this study were isolated from mice 6–7 days post-infection, a time when some anti-parasite antibody may be present on the iRBC surface
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: No defect in B cell binding of iRBCs was observed in vitro when iRBCs were isolated from μMT mice (which lack antibodies) or when an Fc receptor-blocking antibody was added.
source: however, we did not observe any defect in B cell binding of iRBCs in vitro when we isolated iRBCs from μMT mice (which lack antibodies) or added an Fc receptor-blocking antibody (data not shown).
evidence: Based on unpublished experimental data

claim: Malaria has detrimental effects on antibody responses to immunization.
source: One key aspect of our study with relevance for human health is its insight into the detrimental effects of ongoing Plasmodium infection on antibody responses to immunization.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: Poor responses to childhood vaccinations in children from endemic regions have been appreciated for decades.
source: Such effects have been appreciated for decades, most notably through measurement of poor responses to childhood vaccinations in children from endemic regions (Greenwood et al., 1972; Williamson and Greenwood, 1978; Banga et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Greenwood et al., 1972; Williamson and Greenwood, 1978; Banga et al., 2015

claim: Malaria may affect antibody avidity.
source: Malaria also may affect antibody avidity (Cadman et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cadman et al., 2008

claim: Increased turnover of serum antibodies is a contributing factor to malaria-associated decreases in antibody titers.
source: But the mechanisms underlying these malaria-associated decreases in antibody titers have mostly remained unknown, although one paper did identify increased turnover of serum antibodies as a contributing factor (Sardinha et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sardinha et al., 2002

claim: Blood-stage-induced inflammation disrupts the development of sporozoite-specific B cells and antibodies in mice.
source: We recently found that blood-stage-induced inflammation disrupts the development of sporozoite-specific B cells and antibodies in mice (Keitany et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Keitany et al., 2016

claim: CSP-specific memory B cells are relatively scarce in naturally exposed humans.
source: perhaps providing an explanation for the relative scarcity of CSP-specific memory B cells in naturally exposed humans (Wipasa et al., 2010; Jahnmatz et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wipasa et al., 2010 and Jahnmatz et al., 2022

claim: Immunization with adjuvanted protein during acute Plasmodium infection activates immunogen-specific CD4+ T cells, but fails to elicit the Tfh cells necessary to support a robust immunogen-specific B cell response.
source: In the present study, we have further elucidated the cellular basis for defective antibody production during malaria: we showed that immunization with adjuvanted protein during acute Plasmodium infection activates immunogen-specific CD4+ T cells, but fails to elicit the Tfh cells necessary to support a robust immunogen-specific B cell response, correlating with diminished B cell expansion and decreased serum antibody titers.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5

claim: The detrimental effect of Plasmodium infection on antibody production is transient.
source: The detrimental effect on antibody production is transient, suggesting that interactions between B and T cells eventually recover as the infection is cleared to sub-patent levels.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5

claim: Interactions between B and T cells eventually recover as the infection is cleared to sub-patent levels.
source: The detrimental effect on antibody production is transient, suggesting that interactions between B and T cells eventually recover as the infection is cleared to sub-patent levels.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5

claim: Many clinically immune humans carry patent levels of parasites in their blood during much of the year in endemic areas.
source: However, in endemic areas, many clinically immune humans carry patent levels of parasites in their blood during much of the year (Ryg-Cornejo et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ryg-Cornejo et al., 2016b

claim: A strategy in which vaccine is administered together with anti-Plasmodium chemoprophylaxis has recently shown great promise.
source: Even so, a strategy in which vaccine is administered together with anti-Plasmodium chemoprophylaxis has recently shown great promise (Chandramohan et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chandramohan et al., 2021

claim: P. chabaudi exports membrane proteins that render iRBCs cytoadherent.
source: Like P. falciparum, P. chabaudi exports membrane proteins that render iRBCs cytoadherent (Stephens et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Stephens et al., 2012

claim: Cytoadherence was found to be important for interaction with (and suppression of) DCs in one study.
source: a characteristic found to be important for interaction with (and suppression of) DCs in one study (Urban et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Urban et al., 1999

claim: Plasmodium-specific T cell differentiation is under way at 5 days post-infection.
source: At this timepoint, Plasmodium-specific T cell differentiation is under way (Arroyo and Pepper, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Arroyo and Pepper, 2020

claim: Germinal centers are delayed in malaria relative to their kinetics following protein immunization and have not yet formed at 5 days post-infection.
source: but germinal centers, which are delayed in malaria relative to their kinetics following protein immunization, have not yet formed (Krishnamurty et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krishnamurty et al., 2016

claim: Transgenic CD4+ T cells specific for the shed portion of the parasite coat protein MSP1 are capable of assisting B cells in antibody production.
source: Stephens et al. have reported that transgenic CD4+ T cells specific for the shed portion of the parasite coat protein MSP1 are capable of assisting B cells in antibody production (Stephens et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Stephens et al., 2005

claim: P. chabaudi parasitemia is cleared to sub-patent levels roughly 3 weeks after infection, although a low-grade chronic infection persists for several months.
source: This timepoint corresponds roughly to the time that P. chabaudi parasitemia is cleared to sub-patent levels, although a low-grade chronic infection persists for several months in this model (Stephens et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stephens et al., 2012
